title: Uhud: the archers
hook: the archers are told not to leave their hill, even if they see birds snatching the army; they leave for the spoils, and the victory turns (3:152; Bukhari)

segments.voice: Yesterday, mahr: a coat of armor for a bride's gift, and a home of very few things. Your line was: a simple wedding. What did you cut from a plan that had grown too big? Day seven hundred seventy-nine.

Even if you see birds snatching us, don't leave this place until I send for you. That's the order, as Sahih al-Bukhari reports it, in close paraphrase. The Meccans have come back after Badr, to the foot of a mountain outside Medina called Uhud. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ places a company of archers on a small hill, under a companion named Abdullah ibn Jubayr, to guard the army's back. The order couldn't be clearer. Stay. Whatever you see, stay. Today: Uhud.
screen: `EVEN IF YOU SEE BIRDS SNATCHING US.` → `DON'T LEAVE THIS PLACE.` → `UNTIL I SEND FOR YOU.`

segments.voice: At first, the battle goes the Muslims' way. In Bukhari's report, the Meccan line breaks and starts to run. From the hill, the archers can see it: the enemy fleeing, the camp left behind, everything there for the taking. And some of them start calling out: the spoils, the spoils! Your companions have won, what are you waiting for? Abdullah ibn Jubayr reminds them: have you forgotten what the Messenger of Allah told you? They answer that they'll go down to the people and take their share. And they go. The hill is left nearly empty, and the battle turns. In the confusion, Muslims are killed, and the Prophet himself is wounded. Surah Al Imran tells this moment without softening it. Allah kept His promise to you, the verse says, when you were driving them back, until your courage failed, and you argued about the order, and you disobeyed, after He had shown you what you longed for. Then a short line that names the whole thing, in Pickthall's words: "Some of you desired the world, and some of you desired the Hereafter." That's the hill and the valley, in one sentence. The verse doesn't name names. It says some, and some, in one army, on one afternoon. And then the verse does something surprising. After all that, it says Allah has forgiven them. In Bukhari's report, the archers thought the job was done: your companions have won, they said, and their share was waiting below. Some Muslim teachers tell Uhud to name a very ordinary temptation: leaving your post a little early, because the reward is right there and the work looks finished.
screen: `THE MECCAN LINE BREAKS.` · `THE SPOILS, THE SPOILS!` · `HAVE YOU FORGOTTEN WHAT HE TOLD YOU?` · `THE WORLD, OR THE HEREAFTER.` · then, large: `STAY ON THE HILL.`

segments.voice: The practice: finish your duty before your share. Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of one place where you've been asked to hold a post: a child you're watching, a shift you're covering, a promise to a friend, a task someone is counting on. Now notice the pull toward the valley: the phone, the reward, the moment you can call it done before it is. You don't have to fight it. Just see it clearly, the way the archers could see the spoils. Then, in your mind, stay on the hill one breath longer. If you pray, you can ask Allah for steadiness. If you don't, simply rest in the choice. The bell holds the time.
Uhud: the mountain outside Medina where a victory turned, after archers left their hill for the spoils, and the verse that named it and forgave them. Today's word.
Your line: stay on the hill. Today, when something you're responsible for looks finished, give it five more minutes before you go for your share. Day seven hundred seventy-nine.

howItsDone: Muslims read the Uhud passage of Surah Al Imran as a lesson in obedience and forgiveness, and the story of the archers is a common theme in sermons and sirah classes.

fork.setup: you're Abdullah ibn Jubayr, in charge of the archers. the enemy is running, and your men start down the hill toward the spoils. what do you do?
options: go down with them; the battle's won.
remind them of the Prophet's order.
leave the hill to ask the Prophet what to do.
fork.reveal: he asked them: have you forgotten what the Messenger of Allah told you? they went down anyway, and the battle turned.

original.note: Arabic: the name of the mountain outside Medina where the battle was fought.

trapdoor: what you thought: a battle the Muslims lost.
what it means: a victory that turned when people left their post early, and a verse that forgave them.
what a scholar hears: 3:152's courage failing, the argument over the order, the world and the Hereafter, and Bukhari 3039's birds.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 3039 (the archers under Abdullah ibn Jubayr; 'even if you see birds snatching us'; 'the spoils')

notes: Pickthall 3:152 phrase quoted from memory; confirm exact wording ('Some of you desired the world, and some of you desired the Hereafter.'). The rest of the verse is paraphrased.
Bukhari 3039 gives the number of archers (fifty); it is left out here under the claims rule.
'The Meccan horsemen ride around behind it' summarizes the sirah accounts (Khalid ibn al-Walid's cavalry) and Bukhari's report that the battle turned; confirm.
'Some Muslim teachers tell Uhud...' is a general description; confirm it's fair.
The practice mentions asking for steadiness in general terms, not a new prayer.

Editor: cut 'the Meccan horsemen see the gap, ride around behind it' (from the sirah, not the cited Bukhari 3039 or 3:152); the teach now says only that the hill was left nearly empty and the battle turned. Added Bukhari 4075 as the source for the Prophet's wound.

Audit: 'the same people, pulled two ways at once' misread 3:152, whose 'some of you... and some of you' names two groups; rewritten to follow the verse. The narrator's verdict 'the archers weren't wicked' now attributed to the archers' own words in Bukhari 3039.
